learningObjectives.title: Characters (Romeo, Juliet, Mercutio, the Nurse, Friar Lawrence)

questions.q: In which Italian city is 'Romeo and Juliet' set?
questions.explain: The play is set in Verona, though Romeo is later banished to Mantua.

questions.q: What does the Prologue, spoken by the Chorus, reveal at the very start of the play?
options: That the lovers will take their own lives
That the feud will be peacefully resolved
That Romeo will be banished to Mantua
That Juliet will be forced to marry Paris
questions.explain: The Prologue tells us the 'star-cross'd lovers take their life', foreshadowing the tragic ending.

questions.q: Who kills Mercutio in Act 3, Scene 1?
questions.explain: Tybalt fatally wounds Mercutio under Romeo's arm during the street brawl.

questions.q: In revenge for his friend's death, whom does Romeo kill?
questions.explain: Enraged by Mercutio's death, Romeo kills Tybalt, leading to his banishment.

questions.q: How does Romeo die in the Capulet tomb?
options: He stabs himself with a dagger
He is killed by the Prince's guards
questions.explain: Believing Juliet dead, Romeo drinks poison bought from the apothecary.

questions.q: How does Juliet take her own life?
options: She stabs herself with Romeo's dagger
She takes an overdose of the sleeping potion
questions.explain: Waking to find Romeo dead, Juliet stabs herself with his dagger.

questions.q: Which character cries 'A plague o' both your houses' as he dies?
questions.explain: Mercutio curses both the Montagues and Capulets, blaming the feud for his death.

questions.q: What key action does Friar Lawrence perform for Romeo and Juliet?
options: He tells the Prince of the feud
questions.explain: Friar Lawrence marries the couple, hoping their union will end the family feud.

questions.q: The Prologue calls Romeo and Juliet 'star-cross'd lovers'. Which theme does this phrase most directly introduce?
questions.explain: 'Star-cross'd' suggests their love is doomed by destiny, foregrounding the theme of fate.

questions.q: Act 3, Scene 1 (the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt) is often described as the play's turning point because it:
options: Shifts the play from comedy towards tragedy
Introduces the feud for the first time
Resolves the conflict between the families
Delays the marriage of Romeo and Juliet
questions.explain: These deaths and Romeo's banishment mark the structural turn from comic to tragic action.

questions.q: When Friar Lawrence warns 'These violent delights have violent ends', he is:
options: Foreshadowing the tragic outcome of the lovers' passion
Praising the intensity of young love
questions.explain: The line foreshadows how the couple's intense love will end in violence and death.

questions.q: What is the Nurse's main dramatic function in the play?
options: She acts as Juliet's confidante and provides comic moments
questions.explain: The Nurse is Juliet's trusted, often bawdy and comic, confidante and go-between.

questions.q: Juliet's line 'Deny thy father and refuse thy name' most clearly explores the tension between:
questions.explain: Juliet wishes Romeo could reject his Montague name, showing love in conflict with family allegiance.

questions.q: In what verse form is the opening Prologue written?
questions.explain: The Prologue is a fourteen-line sonnet, linking its form to the play's love theme.

questions.q: Mercutio's 'Queen Mab' speech mainly reveals his:
options: Witty, cynical imagination and mockery of dreams
questions.explain: The fanciful Queen Mab speech shows Mercutio's playful wit and scepticism about dreams and love.

questions.q: In 'wherefore art thou Romeo?', the word 'wherefore' means:
questions.explain: Juliet asks why Romeo must be a Montague, not where he is.

questions.q: A student argues that fate controls the tragedy. Which quotation best supports this reading?
options: Romeo's cry 'O, I am fortune's fool!'
Mercutio's 'A plague o' both your houses'
The Nurse's advice to marry Paris
questions.explain: Romeo feels toyed with by fortune after killing Tybalt, directly supporting a fate-driven reading.

questions.q: Which moment best illustrates the theme of youthful haste in the play?
options: Romeo and Juliet agreeing to marry the day after they first meet
Friar Lawrence gathering herbs in his cell
questions.explain: Their rush to marry within a day dramatises the theme of impulsive youth.

questions.q: Which plot event most directly causes the final tragedy by preventing Romeo from learning the truth?
options: Friar Lawrence's letter fails to reach Romeo
Juliet refuses to drink the potion
The Nurse tells Romeo of the plan
Paris warns Romeo at the tomb
questions.explain: Because the letter explaining Juliet's feigned death never arrives, Romeo believes she is truly dead.

questions.q: If asked how Mercutio's death shapes Romeo, the best analysis is that it:
options: Provokes Romeo into killing Tybalt, sealing his banishment
Convinces Romeo to reconcile the families
questions.explain: Grief and rage at Mercutio's death drive Romeo to kill Tybalt, triggering his exile and the tragic chain of events.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE English Literature (1ET0) specification; Romeo and Juliet
